unit.name: Contemporary Issues in Sport
unit.subtitle: Participation, values, ethics, hosting major events, the role of NGBs, and the use of technology — the externally assessed paper covering the social and ethical landscape of modern sport.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer with informal labels ('old people', 'kids', 'disabled') instead of the specification's twelve named user groups. Examiners credit only the spec wording — 'retired people / people over 60', 'young children', 'people with disabilities'. Always teach the closed list verbatim.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR Cambridge National in Sport Studies J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 1.1 (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

common_misconceptions.topic: Pairing a barrier with a matched solution
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list barriers and list solutions but do not pair them. R184 question stems typically read 'Identify one barrier to participation for {user group} and suggest one solution to overcome that barrier' — the mark is awarded for the linkage, not for two separate lists. Always teach barriers → solutions as paired chains keyed to user groups.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR Sample Assessment Material for R184/01 Contemporary Issues in Sport (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610867-contemporary-issues-in-sport.pdf)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix up the value sets. Olympic = Excellence, Friendship, Respect (three). Paralympic = Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality (four). They are not interchangeable and the spec wording must be reproduced exactly.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 2.2.1 (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate the two. Sportsmanship = playing within the letter AND spirit of the sport. Gamesmanship = bending the rules for advantage without breaking them. R184 frequently asks for one applied example of each — teach with paired examples (e.g. kicking the ball out for an injured opponent vs time-wasting at a throw-in).
common_misconceptions.source: OCR J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 2.4 (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

common_misconceptions.topic: WADA's role and the Whereabouts Rule
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name WADA but cannot explain the Whereabouts Rule (athletes in the testing pool must report their location for one hour per day so unannounced out-of-competition testing can occur). Examiners flag this as the most reliably weak knowledge point on the doping topic. Teach the rule mechanically — quarterly Whereabouts submissions, three missed tests or filing failures in 12 months trigger a violation.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Anti-Doping — Whereabouts and ADAMS page (https://www.ukad.org.uk/education/athletes/elite/whereabouts/) and OCR J829 specification 2.5.3.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students invert the three event types — calling Wimbledon 'one-off' or the Olympics 'regular'. The spec definitions are: one-off (host city once in a generation, e.g. Olympic/Paralympic games), regular (held repeatedly but in a different host each time, e.g. UEFA Champions League Final), regular and recurring (held repeatedly at the same venue, e.g. Wimbledon, Monaco GP). Always anchor each category to its spec example.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 3.1.1 (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students given an 'Evaluate the legacy of a major sporting event' question write only positives or only negatives. The spec is explicit — content includes both positive aspects and negative aspects, and high-tariff legacy questions require both sides plus a substantiated judgement. Teach an evaluation scaffold: positive(s), negative(s), counter-point, judgement linked to the question stem.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR Sample Assessment Material for R184/01 Section C extended-response indicative content (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610867-contemporary-issues-in-sport.pdf)

common_misconceptions.topic: NGB functions — naming a real body
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students refer to 'the NGB' generically in answers and lose marks for missing the 'named NGB with sporting examples' requirement. Always teach with concrete NGBs students will recognise — The FA (football), RFU (rugby union), ECB (cricket), LTA (tennis) — and pair functions to that NGB's recent activity.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 4.1 'Breadth and depth' note (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe a piece of technology (VAR, Hawk-Eye) but do not evaluate its positive AND negative effects on the sport, the official and the spectator. The spec splits effects into three lenses (performance, officiating, spectatorship) and high-tariff questions reward students who address more than one lens.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR J829 specification section 4.2 Unit R184 Topic Area 5.2 (https://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/610953-specification-cambridge-nationals-sport-studies-j829.pdf)

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice (Section A): Generally well answered — examiner reports note that Section A MCQs across Q1-Q4 are reliably scored. Trap distractors usually swap a barrier-solution pairing or mis-name an Olympic/Paralympic value.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State Two: Students give two near-identical points rather than two distinct ones (e.g. 'lack of transport' and 'lack of buses') and lose the second mark. Always teach 'two genuinely different points' as the heuristic.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Explain: Students state without explaining. The mark scheme typically demands a point + a reason or a point + an applied example. Always finish with 'because…' or 'for example…'.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Describe with Example: Students describe without anchoring to a named sport, athlete, event or NGB. R184 marks are reliably lost when the spec's 'applied example' requirement is missed. Always demand a named example in the answer.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Discuss: Students list points without making them interact. 'Discuss' demands consideration of more than one viewpoint — two contrasting effects, two stakeholder perspectives, or a positive vs negative side. Always teach a 'two sides + linkage' template.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Evaluate (Extended Response, S: Three failure modes documented in examiner reports: (1) one-sided answers, (2) no judgement at the end, (3) no applied example. The mark scheme uses banded indicative content — Band 3 requires balanced points, judgement and applied example. Always teach the evaluation scaffold.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper is 70 marks, 1h 15m. Section A = 30 marks (MCQ + short answer across all topic areas), Section B = 28 marks (context-based scenarios), Section C = 12 marks (extended-response evaluation).

Topic Area 1 (Issues affecting participation) and Topic Area 3 (Hosting major events) typically carry the most marks each series — they have the most teaching content in the spec and the most evaluation potential.
Topic Area 4 (NGBs) is the lightest topic in the spec — one specification page. Combine into a single lesson rather than padding to fill space.
Topic Area 5 (Technology) is also light but pairs naturally with NGBs (both regulatory/development-of-sport themed). Combined lesson works.
current_spec_changes: Specification version 5 (September 2025) is the live version of J829 — confirm latest before each major rebuild.
Section 2.1 wording: 'Tolerance AND Respect' is treated as ONE sporting value, not two separate ones. Older textbooks split them — current spec does not.

Examples used in lessons (especially emerging sports L3, host events L8/L9, doping cases L7, technology L10) will date quickly. Set a refresh cadence of every 2-3 years — flag this in the content prompt.
pedagogical_notes: EEF cognitive-science guidance: retrieval practice is high-leverage for the closed-list memorisation in R184 (12 user groups, 9 barriers, 7 values, Olympic/Paralympic values, NGB functions). Flashcards and quick-quizzes should hit these list-memorisation hotspots explicitly.

Dual coding: the relationship between barriers and solutions (1.2 → 1.3) is a natural two-column visual. So is positive/negative event impacts (3.3) and positive/negative technology effects (5.2). Build content with these visual structures in mind even where diagrams are not generated (free-tier).

Vocational pedagogy: R184 is application-heavy. Every concept lesson should close with a 'Try this in context' moment — a short scenario applying the new knowledge — because Section B is entirely scenario-based.

Currency matters: this is a contemporary-issues paper. Lessons must use examples from the last 5 years (Paris 2024, current Premier League VAR policy, current UKAD sanctions, current emerging sports). Outdated examples (Beijing 2008 as a 'recent' Olympics) signal the resource is stale and undermine credibility.

lessons_in_batch.title: Etiquette, Sportsmanship & Spectator Behaviour
lessons_in_batch.description: Why performers observe etiquette, the difference between sportsmanship and gamesmanship, and how spectators carry responsibility for safe sporting environments.
lessons_in_batch.adaptation_notes: GCSE PE covers sportsmanship vs gamesmanship in similar terms and that concept transfers as a teaching reference. R184 adds an explicit spectator-behaviour strand (safety, jeopardising fellow spectators) which PE does not, and pins everything to applied examples. Rewrite from spec; lift only the sportsmanship/gamesmanship contrast pattern from PE.

lessons_in_batch.title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
lessons_in_batch.description: Why athletes use PEDs and why they shouldn't, the role of WADA and the Whereabouts Rule, plus sanctions and education strategies designed to deter doping.
lessons_in_batch.adaptation_notes: GCSE PE covers types of PEDs (anabolic agents, beta blockers etc) by physiological effect. R184 takes a more sociological angle — WADA's role, the Whereabouts Rule, sanction structures, education strategies. Rewrite to match R184's framing; PE's drug-type taxonomy is not needed (R184 doesn't enumerate drug types in 2.5).

lessons_in_batch.title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding
lessons_in_batch.description: The three event types (one-off, regular, regular & recurring), what bidding entails, and the pre-event positives and negatives a host city must weigh up.
lessons_in_batch.adaptation_notes: GCSE PE does not require students to classify event types or evaluate bidding processes — this is a Cambridge Nationals vocational/event-management strand. Build fresh. Use Paris 2024 (recent one-off) and the rotating Champions League final cities for current applied examples; refresh every two years.

lessons_in_batch.title: Hosting a Major Event — During & After (Legacy)
lessons_in_batch.description: Positive and negative impacts during the event itself, plus the long-term legacy questions of facility reuse, participation, infrastructure and national status.
lessons_in_batch.adaptation_notes: Legacy analysis is the defining R184 evaluation strand and not part of GCSE PE. Examiner-style 8-12 mark evaluation questions live here. Use Paris 2024 cost overruns (EUR 3.6bn to 8.8bn) and London 2012 long-term legacy as paired contrasting examples; Athens 2004 as the cautionary tale. Refresh as new mega-events are awarded/concluded.

lessons_in_batch.title: National Governing Bodies & Technology in Sport
lessons_in_batch.description: What NGBs do for their sport, plus the role of technology — enhancing performance, increasing safety, supporting officials and shaping the spectator experience.
lessons_in_batch.adaptation_notes: GCSE PE covers technology in sport in similar evaluation terms (positives vs negatives, applied examples). NGB content is lighter in PE — used mainly in context of funding pathways. Combine the two short R184 topic areas (4.1 + 5.1/5.2) into one lesson because each is shallow individually. Lift PE's positive/negative analysis pattern, refresh examples (current VAR Premier League policy, Hawk-Eye in tennis and cricket DRS).
